cues.text: Think about the last time your workday went sideways.
Maybe it was information you needed and couldn't find. A system that made you type the same thing twice.
An approval that sat in somebody's inbox for three days while a customer waited.
Now hold that moment in your mind, because we're going to ask an uncomfortable question about it.
Was that a lazy person problem — or a badly designed process problem?
Most of us are trained to answer that question with a name. Someone dropped the ball. Someone didn't check.
Over the next few minutes I want to show you why that answer is usually wrong, and why the alternative is far more useful to you.
This is the finding that started modern quality thinking.
W. Edwards Deming, working with Japanese manufacturers after the second world war, put a number on it:
about ninety-four percent of performance problems come from the system — the way the work is designed and managed.
Only about six percent come from what he called special causes: one person, one machine, one unusual day.
Two honesty notes before we go on. The exact numbers are a rule of thumb, not a measurement; Joseph Juran had earlier put it at eighty-five and fifteen.
And Deming was making a technical point about two kinds of variation, which you'll meet properly at Yellow Belt.
But the direction is what matters, and on the direction the evidence has been remarkably consistent for seventy years.
When something goes wrong at work, the way the work is set up is the overwhelming favourite. The person is the long shot.
So here is the shift that every improvement method is built on, and it fits on one line: blame the process, not the person.
Then fix the process.
I want to be careful here, because this is often misheard in two directions.
It does not mean nobody is ever accountable for anything. And it does not mean people are helpless.
What it means is narrower and more practical. When you are staring at a problem that keeps happening, the most productive first question is not who did this.
It is: what about the way this work is set up made that likely?
That question is worth learning to ask out loud, because it changes what a room does next.
There are two reasons to work this way, and the first one is simply that it is more accurate.
Think about what happens when a recurring problem gets treated as a people problem. The person is coached, or moved, or replaced.
And then the next person arrives — conscientious, well-intentioned, new — and inherits the same layout, the same forms,
the same two systems that don't talk to each other. Within a few weeks, the same thing goes wrong again.
That pattern is the single most reliable signal you will learn to spot.
If a problem survives a change of personnel, the problem was never in the personnel.
It is built into the work, waiting for whoever shows up next.
The second reason matters even more, and it has nothing to do with being nice.
Think about what you do when you make a mistake somewhere that treats mistakes as personal failures. You fix it quietly. You work around it.
You do not raise it in a meeting. That is not a character flaw — it is a completely rational response to the situation.
Now think about what that means for the organisation. Every hidden problem is a problem nobody can fix,
and it keeps costing money and time and goodwill in the dark.
This is why the language matters. When problems are framed as flaws in how work is designed, people will tell you about them —
because there is nothing personal to defend.
A workplace that hides its problems cannot improve. It's that simple.
Let's make this concrete, because the pattern looks identical in wildly different places.
On a packing line, someone keeps shipping the wrong variant of a product.
Look at the station: two nearly identical bins, side by side, with small labels. A new packer will make that same error inside a week.
On a hospital ward, a nurse "forgets" a discharge step.
Look at the work: the checklist lives in one system and the nurse charts in another. Nothing about that arrangement helps anyone remember anything.
In an office, an analyst sends out figures that turn out to be stale.
Look at the folder: there are three files with "final" in the name and nothing at all marking which one is current.
In every one of those cases, replacing the person changes nothing.
Changing the bins, the systems, the file naming — that changes everything. Same story, three industries.
You will start seeing it everywhere, and that is the point.
Now it's your turn, and this is the part of the module that does the real work.
Think of one thing that goes wrong repeatedly in your own job. Write it down twice.
First as a person problem — the way it probably gets discussed today.
Then as a process problem — what about the setup makes it likely?
Then read both back and ask yourself which version hands you something you could actually change.
There is no scoring here and nobody is grading your writing. Take the time.
Three things to carry out of this module.
First: most recurring problems are built into the process, so changing people rarely fixes them.
Second: framing problems as process flaws is what makes them safe to surface — and a surfaced problem is the raw material of every improvement you will ever make.
Third, and this is the one I'd ask you to hold onto: your frustrations are data.
This course is going to teach you how to read them.
Next up: what a process actually is.
